headline: High: OpenMetadata’s MCP/webhook surfaces and Chatwoot’s broad egress create default-path data leakage and cascading-error risk; prompt-injection risk is lower but present via shared content flows.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Chatwoot can ingest external messages and integrations, while OpenMetadata exposes MCP/APIs/webhooks that can carry attacker-controlled content into workflows. The pair lacks documented provenance or isolation, so prompt-like instruction injection is plausible through shared content paths. Uncertainty about the exact bridge escalates above low.
conditions: IF Chatwoot ingests OpenMetadata webhook or MCP payloads as trusted text
IF either agent forwards untrusted content into downstream tool prompts without sanitization
mitigations: Disable any webhook-to-chat routing that copies raw payloads
Add provenance tags to all cross-agent messages
Strip instructions from imported text before display
Require human review for any content that triggers actions
requires-engineering: enforce schema-validated message boundaries

B_data_leakage.rationale: Chatwoot touches customer data, contact profiles, orders, messages, and reports, and it has broad network egress. OpenMetadata touches governance, lineage, and memory/tribal-knowledge data and exposes APIs, SDKs, events, webhooks, and MCP. In a shared workflow, sensitive data can flow from one into the other and then out over networked integrations by default.
conditions: IF Chatwoot forwards customer records into OpenMetadata metadata or events
IF OpenMetadata webhooks or MCP tools receive customer-support content
IF either agent is connected to third-party integrations without filtering
mitigations: Restrict shared fields to non-sensitive metadata
Block customer data from webhook payloads
Turn off unnecessary outbound integrations
Review logs for accidental PII propagation
requires-engineering: add DLP/redaction at the integration boundary

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Chatwoot has broad network egress and OpenMetadata supports multiple instances plus APIs/SDKs/events/webhooks/MCP, so both can mutate shared external resources if wired together. The profiles do not show shared filesystem writes, but overlapping mutable network surfaces create coordination risk in default integration-heavy setups.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same external ticketing, metadata, or webhook-backed resource
IF no locking or idempotency is configured on shared endpoints
mitigations: Assign separate service accounts
Add idempotency keys to writes
Serialize writes through one orchestrator
Pause one agent during bulk syncs
requires-engineering: implement resource-level locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: Chatwoot can surface customer-facing content and OpenMetadata can publish governance or lineage facts through APIs and webhooks. If OpenMetadata output is treated as authoritative by Chatwoot workflows, errors can cascade into customer communications or operational actions. The interaction is inferred, but the default integration surfaces make the blast radius potentially irreversible.
conditions: IF Chatwoot uses OpenMetadata output to draft or send customer-facing messages
IF OpenMetadata facts are consumed without verification before action
mitigations: Require human approval before outbound messages
Cross-check metadata facts against source systems
Limit OpenMetadata-fed fields to read-only display
Add confidence labels to imported facts
requires-engineering: build verification gates before action-taking

E_compliance.rationale: Chatwoot clearly touches customer data and interaction history, while OpenMetadata handles governance and lineage data. The profiles do not specify residency or certification mismatches, so a concrete breach cannot be proven; however, if customer data is routed into OpenMetadata’s APIs/webhooks, retention and subject-rights handling can diverge. Uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF customer data from Chatwoot is stored in OpenMetadata governance or lineage records
IF the two systems apply different retention or deletion policies to the same records
mitigations: Classify which fields may cross systems
Exclude direct identifiers from metadata syncs
Document retention ownership per system
Run a deletion test on one sample record
requires-engineering: align retention and export workflows
